_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 3 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 2 Concise Algorithms. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order (efficient means concise; cutting the waste, in the lesson's own cake and present; the steps that repeat, in its three plants and its table for four; why concise is better). THE COMPARISON IS THE WHOLE LESSON, so every before-and-after is drawn by handing the LESSON'S OWN scene both lists - ART.scene(cake, ...) and ART.scene(present, ...) - and the film's pictures file asserts at load that the long list and the short list draw the same cake and the same present, aria-label aside. Every count said out loud (ten, seven, nine, six, eleven, five, eighteen, six) is the number of rows actually drawn.
title: Concise Algorithms
subtitle: Grade 3 Computing
objectives: Understand that efficient algorithms are concise.
Identify steps that are repeated within everyday tasks.
Follow, understand, edit and correct linear algorithms.

beats.say: This list has ten steps. This one has seven. Both bake the same cake.
The seven-step one is concise. It does the whole job with no waste.
Efficient means doing the whole job with no waste.
Open the door. Open the door. Walk in. The door is already open.
Step two is waste. Cut it, and you still walk in.
Get a cup. Wave at the cat. Pour the juice. The wave does nothing for the juice.
Cut the wave, and the juice still gets poured. That is concise.
Here is an algorithm for baking a cake. It has ten steps.

at.algorithm: an algorithm for baking a cake

beats.say: Phone a friend is a nice call, but it does nothing for the cake.
Mix it all together. Mix it again, the same way. It is already mixed.
The second mix is waste. So is the funny hat. Cut all three.
Ten steps became seven, and every one of the seven does something.
Ask it of every step: cut this, and does the cake still get baked?
Now wrap a present for Nora. Nine steps, with waste in them.
Wrap the box in paper. Unwrap it to check the teddy. Wrap it again.
Those two steps undo each other. Cut both, and the paper stays on.
Counting to one hundred does nothing for the present. Cut that too.
Nine steps became six: box, lid, paper, tape, ribbon, tag.
Water three plants. Fill the can, pour on a plant, walk to the next one.
That run of three steps comes round again for the second plant, and for the third.
Written out long, that is eleven steps on the page.
Instead, write the run once and say repeat three times.
Eleven steps become five, and the three plants still get watered.
Laying the table for four is the same. Plate, fork, knife, cup, four times over.
Eighteen steps become six with a repeat.
A concise algorithm is easier to follow, because there is less to read.
It is easier to understand, because every step matters.
And it is easier to edit. Change the repeated run once, and all three change.
Computers like it too. Fewer steps is less work.
An efficient algorithm is concise: only the steps the task needs.
Waste is a step done twice, or one that does nothing at all.
Steps that come round again are written once with a repeat.
